idiom_name: hand-written parser methods over a token list with switch-expression dispatch (Roslyn-shaped)
implementation_notes: The .NET base class library ships no parser, and the C# compiler itself is the model: Roslyn's LanguageParser is a hand-written parser with one method per grammar production, an explicit recursion-depth counter, terminator state used for error recovery and a full-fidelity token list. In application code the shape is a sealed token record or struct with position, a Parser class holding the token list and an index, peek/expect helpers that throw a positioned ParseError, methods returning node records, and switch expressions over token kinds for dispatch. What replaces the classic structure is nothing - C# makes the hand-written form pleasant but does not remove it - so use the hand-written parser for grammars you own, and Roslyn's Syntax API (CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText, SyntaxNode, SyntaxToken) when the input is C# or VB itself.
pitfalls: Roslyn tracks a recursion depth counter and terminator state to recover; a parser that skips both turns pathological nesting into a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught in .NET.
Allocating a record per token makes the token list the parse's dominant allocation; a struct token or a green/red tree (as Roslyn uses) avoids it when throughput matters.
Throwing on the first mismatch is easy but discards recovery; IDE-grade tooling needs a diagnostics list and nodes synthesised with missing tokens.
